body: Courtney Rozen[ワシントン ６日 ロイター] - ３日の米中間選挙で連邦議会の上下両院で過半数議席を獲得した民主党は、来年１月からの議会で、人工知能（ＡＩ）システムやデータセンター‌開発を対象とする多数の法案を提出する計画だ。議員や議会スタッフ、政策⁠提言に携わる関係者らが明らかにした。共和党主導の議会は主にＡＩ開発の促進に力を入れ、技術の一部を制限する法案の可決を見送ってきた。民主党の計画はこうした方針から​の大きな転換となる。関係者によると、民主党はデータセンターに伴う電気料金の上昇から消費者を守る法案や、先端ＡＩシステムに第三者による検証を義‌務付ける法案、ＡＩ企業が製品による損害の責任を問われる条件を明確にする法案を提出する計画だ。ただトランプ大統領はＡＩ技術への強制力のある規制を求める声を繰り返し退けており、同氏の在‌任中はいずれの法案も成立へのハードル‌は高い。それでも民主党議員や政策提言を行う外部の関係者は、議​会の委員会を握れば、法案の推進や業界首脳への証言の義務付けが可能になり、ＡＩシステムが現実に被害をもたら‌した場合には対策への支持を広げられるとしている。レイモンド・ジェームズの政策調査責任者エド・ミルズ氏は、危機が起きれば、ＡＩ規制‌に反対する大統領を押し切るだけの​支持が集まる可能性があると述べた。「法案が成立する可能性は、人々が予想す‌るよりはるかに高い」と語った。毎年成立させる必要のある定例法案に民主党がＡＩ規制を盛り込もうとする可能性もあると⁠の見方を示した。＜複数の法案提出へ＞上院多数党院内総務に就くとみられる民主党のシューマー上院議員は５日、ワシントンでのイベントで、データセンターの急拡大に伴うエネルギーコストの上昇から消費者を守ることが来年の⁠優先課題の一つになると述べた。民主党のＡＩ政策を代表する議員の一​人であるトラハン下院議員は、‌主要なＡＩモデルが安全基準を満たしているかを独立した専門家に評価させる法案を推進する計画だ。同議員の副首席補佐官フランシス・グルーバー氏が明らかにした。グルーバー氏によると、トラハ⁠ン氏はＡＩシステムが有害な動作をした場合に、企業が責任を問われ得ることを明確にす⁠る法案の成立も目指す。ミシガン州で上院選に当選した民主党のアブドゥル・エルサイド氏は選挙戦で、ＡＩ規制を監督⁠し、ＡＩ開発企業を取り締まる権限を持つ独立機関の設置を訴えた。民主党は新たに得る権限を使い、ＡＩ開発企業のオープンＡＩやアンソロピッ‌クなど、⁠業界で最も強い影響力を持つ企業への監視も強める計画だ。下院科学委員長への就任を目​指す民主党のロフグレン下院議員は、民主党は「イノベーションを促しつつ、責任あるＡＩ規制を整備する」ことに注力すると述べた。

title: 寂しい 地震被災で工場の復旧断念
body:
日本製紙は、今年7月の熊本地震で被災し、工場内で9人が死亡した八代工場について、新聞用紙やパルプ事業を終了する方針を発表しました。【写真を見る】熊本地震で折れた工場の煙突　地域住民の悲痛な声■「元通りの復旧は極めて困難」日本製紙八代工場は、今年7月の地震で煙突3本が被災し、このうち倒壊した1本の下敷きになって従業員9人が亡くなりました。11月6日、東京で開かれた決算説明会の冒頭で、日本製紙の瀬邊社長は八代工場の今後について…日本製紙 瀬邊明社長「工場の被害は非常に甚大かつ工場内の広範囲にわたっていて、残念ながら元に戻す形での復旧は極めて難しいとの判断に至った。グラフィック用紙・パルプ事業は八代工場においては終了します」日本製紙は、熊本地震で151億円の特別損失を計上したと発表しました。八代工場は日本製紙にとって九州で唯一の生産拠点ですが、工場の主要商品であった新聞用紙などのグラフィック用紙やパルプ事業を終了する方針を明らかにしました。八代工場に勤務する約400人の従業員は、グループ内で配置転換するなどして雇用の確保に努めたいとしていて、工場は今後、新事業などの拠点として維持する方針です。日本製紙 瀬邊明社長「長年にわたって築き上げてきた木質資源のサプライチェーンを始めとする事業基盤を生かし、新たな事業の可能性について幅広い分野から協業パートナーを募りながら検討していきたい」ただ、具体的な方向性はこれから決めるということです。■市民の声は──1924年に当時の九州製紙が操業を始めてから100年以上、八代市で紙の生産を続けてきた日本製紙が、この工場での紙やパルプの生産再開を断念したことについて、市民からは地元経済への影響を懸念する声が上がりました。70代男性「地元関連の企業あたりも相当厳しくなるんじゃないですかね。経済的にどう復興していくのかなと」60代女性「そこで仕事をしている人も多いじゃないですか。そうした関連企業の人もいっぱいいるので、生活とか大変だろうなと」
煙突から煙が上がる様子は、八代市のシンボルでもありましたが…八代市在住70代「煙突は八代のシンボルだったから、外に行って帰って来た時煙突を見れば『八代に帰って来たな』と思っていたので。煙突がなくなるのは、やっぱり寂しい」肥後銀行によりますと、今年8月時点で日本製紙の取引先は県内だけで300社以上。関連する従業員は6000人を超え、今回の地震による操業停止が1年間続いた場合、経済損失は約830億円に上る見通しだということです。

title: 中学生4割が外国人増否定的 調査
body: 外国人の増加を「社会にとって良いことが多いと思わない」と考える中学生が、2025年の調査で4割を超え、22年の2割超から倍近くに増加したことが7日、東京大の仁平典宏教授（社会学）の分析で分かった。首都圏の公立中での調査で、ルールを破る人を厳しく罰すべきだと考える生徒が否定的に見る傾向があった。一方で寛容さなど「リベラル的志向」を示す傾向も9割超で、仁平氏は単なる保守化という捉え方はできないと分析。25年の参院選に絡み「外国人は悪さをしているという言説がインターネット上で急に増えた」とし、ウェブの影響を強く反映している可能性を指摘した。調査は首都圏の公立中10校の生徒約2千人を対象に、12年から開始した。主に18～19、22、25年分を分析した。仁平氏によると、過去の調査では、ルールを重視する生徒は外国人増加に肯定的だったが、25年は否定的になり逆転した。「ルールは厳守すべきだ」という価値観が広がっており、それが排外的な志向と結びつきやすくなっているとした。

title: メーガン妃父 ポルノ所持疑い逮捕
body: イギリスのヘンリー王子の妻、メーガン妃の父親が児童ポルノ所持の疑いでFBIに逮捕されました。アメリカ司法省によりますと、フロリダ州に住むメーガン妃の父親、トーマス・マークル容疑者（82）はロサンゼルス郊外で借りていた2つの倉庫に少女たちと容疑者が映ったわいせつな画像を保管していたということです。FBIはそれらの画像など証拠品78点を押収したうえで、6日マークル容疑者を児童ポルノ所持の疑いで逮捕しました。メーガン妃の父親マークル容疑者については先月、メーガン妃の異母兄弟がフィリピンにある容疑者の家で児童のわいせつな画像など数百枚以上を見つけたため、フィリピン警察やFBIなどに通報したとイギリスメディアが報じていました。メーガン妃はヘンリー王子と結婚した2018年以来、父親と疎遠になっています。父親がパパラッチに結婚式前のメーガン妃の写真を撮らせようとしたことが原因とされています。今回の疑惑が報じられた先月、メーガン妃は「ニュースに深く心を痛めており、被害を受けた可能性のある子供たちに思いを馳せています」とコメントしていました。

title: 迷惑行為ショウリンジ 7歳も補導
body:
いま、全国各地で相次いでいる若者たちのある迷惑行為。その迷惑行為とは、交番の前で「少林寺」と叫び、走り去る謎の行為、「少林寺レーシング」。■謎の迷惑行為「少林寺レーシング」の実態その動画は、SNSで瞬く間に拡散しています。【少年の犯罪心理・専門家】「SNS使うことで、世界中からの注目集められる。悪さをするエネルギーになってしまっている」横行する迷惑行為を徹底取材しました。
発端となったのは、SNSに投稿された1本の動画でした。交番に入ろうとする少年らが、突然「ショウリンジじゃー！」と叫びます。別の動画では、少年が「落とし物なんですけど」と交番を訪れ、警察官が「落とし物ありがとうございます」と応じます。落とし物を届けに来たのかと思いきや、少年は「ショウリンジじゃ！」と叫びました。公衆電話で110番を押し、同じ言葉を叫ぶ動画もあります。いわば警察を挑発するこの一連の行為が「少林寺レーシング」です。SNSで検索すると、関連する動画が数多く表示されます。
全国各地で相次ぐ迷惑行為に警察も頭を抱えます。【大阪府警察本部生活安全部少年課 黒木剛調査官】「大阪府内では9月中旬以降、交番に押しかけて『少林寺じゃ』と叫ぶなどの事案が多発しています。少なくても（10月末までで）約280件もの関連事案を認知し、7歳から16歳までの少年約50人を検挙・補導しており、逮捕に至った少年もおります」最年少の補導者は、小学1年生の7歳でした。また、兵庫県警でも、10月下旬までに小学生など25人が検挙・補導されています。少年らは警察の調べに対し、次のように話したといいます。【少年】「学校の友達を笑わすためにやった」【少年】「SNSで動画を見て、警察官をおちょくるのが面白そうだと思った」
11月2日、「少林寺レーシング」と名乗ったSNSアカウントで暴走行為を呼びかける投稿をし、警察の業務を妨害した疑いで、18歳の少年が逮捕されました。この少年のアカウントには、「本家です」「大阪府警公認」といった文言が書かれていました。それでも連鎖は止まっていません。捜査関係者によると、4日の午後7時20分ごろ、関西テレビ近くの交番でも発生したということです。ドライブレコーダーには、複数の警察車両が集まり、交番でも鑑識活動とみられる様子で警察官が動き回る姿が映っていました。当時の状況はこうです。警察官が休憩中の交番に、中学生など4人の少年らがやってきました。少年らはスライドドアを開閉しながら「少林寺レーシング」と叫び、逃走します。3人は補導されましたが、1人は現在も逃走中だといいます。そもそも「少林寺」といえば、武術で有名な中国の寺が思い浮かびます。しかし、いつ誰が始めたのか、「少林寺」との関連も分かっていません。

title: 米大統領首席補佐官 ミラー氏昇格
body: [ワシントン ６日 ロイター] - トランプ米大統領は６日、大統領首席補佐官を務め‌るスージー・ワイルズ氏を自身の政⁠治運営部門に異動させ、次席補佐官のスティーブン・ミラー氏を９日付で首席補佐官​に昇格させる人事を発表した。理由について「変化をもたらしたか‌った」と述べた。トランプ大統領は自身の交流サイト（ＳＮＳ）「トゥルース・ソーシャル」への‌投稿で、ミラー氏を「‌最も信頼する顧問の一人」​と指摘。ワイルズ氏については、政治運営部門（Trump Political Operation）‌に異動するとし、「首席補佐官としての勤務に感謝したい。‌素晴らしい仕事​をしてくれた」と記した。今回の人事は、‌民主党が上下院を支配する議会や、予想される一連⁠の議会調査にトランプ氏が直面する中で、長年の忠実な側近であるミラー氏に政権課題のかじ取り⁠を委ねるものとなる。ホワイトハウ​ス当局者‌はロイターに対し、ミラー氏の起用は、トランプ大統領が国内政策と政治において強硬な姿勢⁠を取ることを示唆していると語った。ミ⁠ラー氏は、トランプ政権の強硬な移民取り締まり⁠を主導し、１日３０００人逮捕という目標を掲げたことでも知られる。別のホ‌ワイ⁠トハウス高官は「大統領は最も忠実な者​たちに報いている。路線を変えるつもりはない」と語った。

title: MAGA連合に亀裂生じる CNN調査
body: （CNN）　2年前にトランプ米大統領の再選を後押ししたMAGA（米国を再び偉大に）運動の連合勢力に亀裂が入り始めていることが、CNNの有権者調査で明らかになった。3日の中間選挙では、従来の共和党王国でも民主党の上院議員候補らが票をさらい、議席を奪っている。【映像】トランプ氏、女性記者に「ブタ、静かに」テキサス、オハイオ、アイオワ、カンザス、サウスカロライナ各州では、中間選挙の有権者のうち、2024年大統領選でトランプ氏に投票したグループが最大の割合を占めていたにもかかわらず、今回の上院選で民主党候補が勝利。5州とも、トランプ氏に投票していた層の1割前後が民主党候補の支持に回った。ジョージア、ノースカロライナの両州でも、大統領選ではトランプ氏に投票した層の1割以上が民主党候補に投票した。トランプ氏は中間選挙に先立ち、これらすべての州を訪問。自分が候補者名簿に載っていると思って投票してほしいと、支持者らにたびたび訴えていた。だがトランプ氏に投票した層で、今回の下院選での投票をトランプ氏への支持を示すメッセージと位置づけていた有権者は約3分の1。トランプ氏は要因にならないとの回答が大半を占めた。大統領選でトランプ氏に票を入れたと自己申告し、今回の中間選挙で投票に出向いた全米の有権者のうち、地元下院選挙区の民主党候補を支持した人は約7％に上った。（これに対し、24年大統領選で民主党候補だったカマラ・ハリス氏に投票した有権者のうち、下院選での投票を反トランプ氏の意思表示と位置づけていた人の割合は4分の3を超え、共和党候補に投票したと答えた人は2％にとどまった）トランプ氏の支持者の中で、中間選挙への熱意ややる気がなく、投票を見送った人々の割合も高かった。中間選挙での全米の有権者のうち、大統領選でトランプ氏に投票していた人の20％が、今は同氏を支持しないと答えた。トランプ氏は自分たちのような国民のために戦っていない、あるいは優先順位が間違っているとの回答も、同様の割合を占めた。こうした回答には、第2期トランプ政権が下した一連の決断に対する不満が反映されている。米国の経済状況が「良くない」「悪い」との回答は約5割、トランプ氏の経済政策が状況を悪化させたとの回答も約27％に上った。対イラン軍事行動の決断が間違いだったと答えた人は、全体の約4分の1。バンス副大統領は4日、中間選挙での共和党の主な敗因としてこの決断を挙げた。CNNの有権者調査は従来の出口調査に代わり、選挙当日の投票所での対面式調査と、選挙前に全米で実施する数万人規模の聞き取り調査を組み合わせる形で、全米の有権者約10万人を対象に実施された。これによって、24年大統領選でトランプ氏を支持した連合勢力を掘り下げることができ、一部の層で第2期トランプ政権の方向性に対する不満が特に大きい傾向が浮き彫りになった。中間選挙の有権者全体の中で、大統領選ではトランプ氏に投票した30歳未満の男性の半分近くが、大統領としての同氏を支持していないと答えた。同様の回答は、トランプ氏に投票していた中南米系有権者の約4分の1、「非MAGA」を名乗る共和党支持者の約3分の1を占めた。トランプ氏の任期切れを2年後に控え、次期大統領選に臨む共和党の後継者が、ひびの入り始めたMAGA連合をまとめ直せるのかどうか、答えはまだ定まっていない。

title: 中間選挙 現状を拒否した無党派層
body:
米国の中間選挙における共和党大敗には、無党派層の影響が無視できない。二大政党制の米国でも、特定の政党に固執しない有権者が近年増えているからだ。
ピュー・リサーチ・センターの最新調査によると、「民主党支持」が29%、「共和党支持」が28%だった一方、それ以外が44%だった。そのなかには「民主党寄り」、「共和党寄り」も含まれる。
手法は異なるがギャロップの調査でも45%が「独立系」と回答している。
政党間のイデオロギー対立が深刻化するなか、これと距離を置く無党派層の増加は、米国政治の影の主役になりつつある。
3日夜に共和党が喫した敗北は、民主党にとって最も楽観的なシナリオさえも超えるレベルの歴史的な大惨敗（後略）出典：ＡＦＰ＝時事　2026/11/5(木)
New High of 45% in U.S. Identify as Political Independents出典：Gallup　2026/1/12(月)
そのトランプはブロンクスの集会で「黒人やヒスパニックが殺されようとしている」と叫び、聴衆の喝采を浴びた。出典：六辻彰二　2024/5/31(金)
Swing voters don't really love Democrats（後略）出典：PBS News　2026/11/4(水)
無党派層の潜在力の大きさは、2024年大統領選挙でもみられた。バイデン政権がガザ侵攻を容認し続けたことをきっかけに、民主党支持が強いとみられていた若者、ヒスパニック、黒人などの一部が流れたことは、トランプ再選の一因になったのだ。
ところが今回の中間選挙で振り子は逆に動いた。たとえばAPによると、30歳以下の有権者の投票は2024年大統領選挙でほぼ半々に割れたが、今回は7割が民主党を支持した。
そこには経済だけでなく政治そのものへの不信感も見受けられる。
議会承認なしに始まったイラン戦争を上下両院で多数派だった共和党が黙認したように、トランプ政権のもとでは議会の独立性が疑問視されやすくなった。これについてAPの事前調査では、有権者の約70%が「議会は政府に対するチェック・アンド・バランスを十分果たしていない」と回答し、共和党支持者でも約40%が同様に回答した。
つまり無党派層の多くは現状を拒否したのであり、民主党を積極的に支持したとは限らない。実際APの調査では、民主党に投票した有権者の約20%は民主党にネガティブな感想を抱いていた。
そのため二大政党は今後ますます無党派層の動向を無視できなくなるといえるだろう。

title: 米民主党 AI規制法案を多数提出へ
body: Courtney Rozen[ワシントン ６日 ロイター] - ３日の米中間選挙で連邦議会の上下両院で過半数議席を獲得した民主党は、来年１月からの議会で、人工知能（ＡＩ）システムやデータセンター‌開発を対象とする多数の法案を提出する計画だ。議員や議会スタッフ、政策⁠提言に携わる関係者らが明らかにした。共和党主導の議会は主にＡＩ開発の促進に力を入れ、技術の一部を制限する法案の可決を見送ってきた。民主党の計画はこうした方針から​の大きな転換となる。関係者によると、民主党はデータセンターに伴う電気料金の上昇から消費者を守る法案や、先端ＡＩシステムに第三者による検証を義‌務付ける法案、ＡＩ企業が製品による損害の責任を問われる条件を明確にする法案を提出する計画だ。ただトランプ大統領はＡＩ技術への強制力のある規制を求める声を繰り返し退けており、同氏の在‌任中はいずれの法案も成立へのハードル‌は高い。それでも民主党議員や政策提言を行う外部の関係者は、議​会の委員会を握れば、法案の推進や業界首脳への証言の義務付けが可能になり、ＡＩシステムが現実に被害をもたら‌した場合には対策への支持を広げられるとしている。レイモンド・ジェームズの政策調査責任者エド・ミルズ氏は、危機が起きれば、ＡＩ規制‌に反対する大統領を押し切るだけの​支持が集まる可能性があると述べた。「法案が成立する可能性は、人々が予想す‌るよりはるかに高い」と語った。毎年成立させる必要のある定例法案に民主党がＡＩ規制を盛り込もうとする可能性もあると⁠の見方を示した。＜複数の法案提出へ＞上院多数党院内総務に就くとみられる民主党のシューマー上院議員は５日、ワシントンでのイベントで、データセンターの急拡大に伴うエネルギーコストの上昇から消費者を守ることが来年の⁠優先課題の一つになると述べた。民主党のＡＩ政策を代表する議員の一​人であるトラハン下院議員は、‌主要なＡＩモデルが安全基準を満たしているかを独立した専門家に評価させる法案を推進する計画だ。同議員の副首席補佐官フランシス・グルーバー氏が明らかにした。グルーバー氏によると、トラハ⁠ン氏はＡＩシステムが有害な動作をした場合に、企業が責任を問われ得ることを明確にす⁠る法案の成立も目指す。ミシガン州で上院選に当選した民主党のアブドゥル・エルサイド氏は選挙戦で、ＡＩ規制を監督⁠し、ＡＩ開発企業を取り締まる権限を持つ独立機関の設置を訴えた。民主党は新たに得る権限を使い、ＡＩ開発企業のオープンＡＩやアンソロピッ‌クなど、⁠業界で最も強い影響力を持つ企業への監視も強める計画だ。下院科学委員長への就任を目​指す民主党のロフグレン下院議員は、民主党は「イノベーションを促しつつ、責任あるＡＩ規制を整備する」ことに注力すると述べた。

title: 米国版凱旋門 ⁠着工一時差し止め
body: David Shepardson[ワシントン ５日 ロイター] - トランプ米大統領がワシントンに建設を計画している高さ７６メ‌ートルの凱旋門について、連邦地裁は５日、⁠着工を一時差し止めた。首都計画委員会が計画を承認した直後だった。チュトカン判事は１４日間の差し止​め命令を出した。これに先立ち、独立行政機関である同委員会は民主党議員ら約１００人‌の反対意見を聞いた上で、賛成８、反対４で計画を承認していた。トランプ政権は、議会が１００年以上前にポトマ‌ック川に架かる橋の建設を‌認めた際に、凱旋門も承認した​と主張している。チュトカン氏は「１００年前の法律が、首都の主要な‌場所に高さ２５０フィートの凱旋門を建てる権限を与えており、歴代のどの政権‌もその権限に気付いて​いなかったとは到底考えにくい」とし「‌そのこと自体が、この計画を正当化するために（政府が）⁠どれほど無理な解釈を強いられているかを示している」と記した。また承認によって約３年間の工事が始まり、「交通の混乱⁠や騒音、大規模な掘削などが生じる」​と指摘した。司法省‌は先に、計画が承認されれば、掘削と基礎工事を中心とする最初の６─８カ月間の工事を早ければ５日に始められるとの⁠見通しを示していた。地上部分の工事は早け⁠れば２０２７年５月に始まり、全体の工期は３３─３９カ月を見込むとしていた。凱旋門の建設計⁠画を巡っては、バージニア州とコロンビア特別区が１０月３１日、着工差し‌止めを求⁠めて国立公園局と内務省を提訴した。計画は「​法的に正当化できない」とし、議会の承認を得ていないと主張した。

title: 米10月雇用16.5万人増 予想上回る
body: アメリカの10月の雇用統計は、景気の動向を敏感に反映する「非農業部門の就業者数」が前の月に比べて16万5000人の増加で、6万5000人程度の増加を見込んでいた市場の予想を大きく上回りました。【画像で見る】激戦州を争った候補たち トランプ政権で中間選挙“大敗”失業率は4.1%で、前の月から0.1ポイント低下しています。市場ではアメリカの中央銀行にあたるFRB＝連邦準備制度理事会が次回、12月の会合で利上げに踏み切る可能性が高いとみられていましたが、今回の雇用統計の結果を受けて、さらに12月利上げの見方が強まりそうです。

title: 信金のシステム障害 すべて復旧
body: 信用金庫のシステムなどを手がける「しんきん共同センター」（東京）は、西日本地域の128の信金で発生したシステム障害が、すべての業務で復旧したと明らかにした。資金決済やATMの利用などが休止していた。原因は「機器の故障によるものだ」としており、サイバー攻撃が原因ではないとの見方を示した。障害があったのは、東海、北陸、近畿、中国、四国、九州（沖縄を除く）の各地域にある128の信金。これらの信金は、しんきん共同センターを通じて10月中旬にシステムを更新していた。障害は午後1時半ごろから起き、オンライン送金やアプリでの取引など複数の業務に影響が出た。大阪市中央区の大阪シティ信用金庫本店では、客から「（ATMは）いつ復旧するんだ」と不満の声が上がった。大阪市の70代男性は「光熱費の引き落としがあるので入金したかった」と話し、足早に立ち去った。

title: 中間選挙ショック 世界で株安連鎖
body: 6日の日経平均株価は、一時4000円急落し、アジアを中心に株安が連鎖しています。今後どういった展開が考えられるのか、フジテレビ・智田裕一解説副委員長と見ていきます。【画像】今後の株価は?解説を見るまず、この株安はアメリカから始まって世界に広がっていきました。アメリカのニューヨーク株式市場では、ダウ平均が1800ドルを超える下落をし、割合で言うと3.44％も下がりました。そしてお隣、韓国の株式市場は8％以上下落して、一時、取引が停止される事態になるほどでした。さらには、台湾でも一時、過去最大となる約9％の下げとなって、いずれもAI関連株を中心に大きな下げとなっているわけです。――急落の原因は、先日のアメリカ中間選挙の共和党の大敗?そうですね。ある意味“中間選挙ショック”といえるかと思います。共和党が負けてアメリカでは株価がいったんは値上がりしたんですが、民主党の躍進でAI投資やデータセンターの建設に規制が強化されるという警戒感が急速に強まったということです。さらに、AIの巨額の投資が本当に利益につながるのかという懸念があります。もともとあったAI需要を巡る懸念を、“中間選挙ショック”がさらに強める形になったということだと思います。――今の値動きは、過去にも似たような事態があった?一部の市場関係者の間で思い起こされているのが、2000年に起きた事態なんです。この時は、インターネットの普及で世界が変わるということで、ITバブルに沸き、株価は2万円を超える水準まで高値を付けました。しかし、バブルがはじけるとIT株を中心に一気に急落したということがありました。――このITバブルの崩壊が、今の動きに似ているという指摘が一部であると?6万円超えが続いていた株価ですが、AI投資の持続性に疑問符が付く中で、ITバブルの時と同じような値下がり基調をたどらないにしても、AIが相場を引っ張っていく力が弱くなっていくかどうかに今、関心が寄せられているということです。街の人は株価の急落をどう捉えているのか、聞いてみました。40代（男性）:かなり不安というか、NISAとかやってる。楽観視はできないけど、また戻ってくるのをじっくり待ちたい。40代（女性）:落ちてる。徐々に落ちてますけど、多少はまた回復していくかと長い目で見て、明るい展望も見据えた上で見ていくことも大事だと思う。20代:（NISA）やってる。今すごく人気あって、今のご時世で株が暴落していることに驚いている。これから回復することを願っている。街の声を聞くと、NISAをやっているという人が多かったですが、ただ結構冷静というか、つみたて投資なので長い目で見ているところもありますよね。現在、NISA口座数で言いますと約2800万というところで、人口で見てみるとざっと国民の4人に1人という割合です。――今回の暴落、急落のNISAへの影響は?NISAで投資信託とか株式を購入している場合、現在の評価額で見た場合は少なからず影響を受けることになりそうです。ただ、NISAのつみたて投資は長期的な資産形成を目的としている部分もあるので、自分のライフプランを踏まえて株式相場の今後の動向を注意深く見ていくことが必要かなと思います。――株価は今後下がり続けていくのか、それともどこかで止まるのか?悪い材料といい材料両方あると思います。悪い材料の1つは民主党がデータセンターなどの規制を強めることで、AI投資の減速につながっていくということ。もう1つは、今後トランプ大統領が対外政策でどのように動くか不確定な要素があるということです。中東情勢の不透明さに加えて、トランプ関税はやめないと本人も言っているので、世界経済に影響を与えることになると思います。トランプ氏の発言も日によってどんどん変わっていったりしているので、全てが不確実要素といえるかもしれません。――いい材料として考えられるのは何?これもAIをめぐるものだと思います。関係者の間からは、暮らしを大きく変えつつあるAIが、この先、着実に普及していき、需要の拡大に見合うだけの投資計画が確実に進んでいく流れが見えてくれば、株価は安定して上昇基調に戻るんじゃないかとの声が上がっています。6日に街の声を聞いた中では、比較的長い目で見ていけばという安心の声もありましたけれども、一方で、この事態を受けて不安に思っている方もいらっしゃるかと思います。今回の急落で改めてリスク分散を考えるきっかけになるかもしれません。

title: KDDI社長 決算会見で2つのおわび
body:
KDDIは11月6日、2027年3月期第2四半期の連結決算を発表した。売上高は前年同期比4.7％増の3兆528億円、営業利益は13.9％増の6331億円となり、各セグメントで増収増益となった。【画像を見る】2027年3月期第2四半期の連結決算モバイル通信などのテレコムコア事業では、1年以内の短期解約率の低下や上位プランの契約増加などから、売上高は前年同期比で3.1％増の2兆2010億円となった。金融事業や「auでんき」などのエネルギー事業を含むパーソナルグロース事業の売上高は同8.3％増の6053億円、データセンターなどAI関連事業を含むビジネスグロース事業は同10.2％増の3309億円だった。
KDDIの松田浩路社長は同日に開催した決算発表会の冒頭で、KDDIの子会社でモンゴルの総合通信事業者であるMobicom Corporation（以下、モビコム）の活動に関連した火災について謝罪した。「当社子会社のモビコムの活動に関連して、10月8日にモンゴルのヌムルグ自然保護区において草原火災が発生いたしました。モンゴル国政府ならびにモンゴルの国民の皆さま、そして長年にわたり両国の友好と歩みを支えてこられた皆さまに多大なる心配とご迷惑をおかけしていることを深くおわび申し上げます。消火活動に当たられた方をはじめ、本件への対応にご尽力いただいている国内外の全ての方に心より感謝を申し上げます」（松田社長）また、説明会の焦点の1つとなったのがサイバー攻撃への対応だ。KDDIでは6月23日、ISP事業者向けに提供しているメールシステムが不正アクセスを受けたと発表した。提供先のISP事業者が手掛ける1223万3087件のメールサービスの情報が漏えいした。松田社長は「高度に技術発展をしてきたにもかかわらず、旧来の方式を運用し、1000万件を超えるメールアドレスを漏えいしてしまいました。この経験を生かすべくサイバーセキュリティ対策にも取り組んでいます」と説明。「情報漏えいなどについて最近でも報告をさせていただいているところです。ご心配をおかけして、大変申し訳ございません」と謝罪した。対策として1つ目に挙げたのが、脆弱（ぜいじゃく）性が見つかった際に必要であればサービス停止をためらわないという経営判断だ。現場では顧客へのサービス提供を続けたいという思いがあるものの、状況に応じてサービスを止め、対応を進めるなど、判断基準をこれまでとは変えていく。2つ目は、万が一侵入された場合でも早期に検知し、被害を最小限に抑える体制の構築だ。松田社長は「当時思ったのは、非常に多くの情報が抜かれたのに、なぜ気付けなかったのかということ」と振り返る。情報漏えいの経験から、検知の遅れが被害を拡大させることを痛感したという。こうした対策の起点となるのが、サイバー脅威の観測・分析をする「脅威インテリジェンス」の取り組みだ。予防、検知、復旧の3つのプロセスでサイバーセキュリティ対策を進める考えだ。

title: 破産手続き中の全東信 社長が死去
body: 破産手続き中の決済代行会社、（株）全東信（TSRコード:575448075、大阪府）の髙山萬保・代表取締役社長が死去した。複数の関係者が東京商工リサーチ（TSR）に明かした。全東信の破産管財人室はTSRの取材に対し、「代表者への聞き取りは不可能になるが、破産手続きへの影響はなく、これまで通り粛々と進められる予定」とコメントした。髙山社長は9月16日付で大阪地裁より破産開始決定を受けている。

title: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
summary: Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat election victory would mean slower AI development.
body:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday,ending the day up 1.1%,partlyreversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies,closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Averagewas flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.
Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
Pierre Baqué, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.
"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.
"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1%from 4.2% in September.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

title: Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race
summary: The buzz about the presidential election is already under way - here's what we learned this week.
body:
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Republican Vice-President JD Vance
Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.
Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.
But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.
No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.
Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.
The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways. Here are four takeaways.
Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.
Georgia Democratic SenatorJon Ossoffwon by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.
While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.
Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania GovernorJosh Shapiro, swept aside his Republican challenger.
Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.
Illinois GovernorJB Pritzkeralso won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.
California GovernorGavin Newsomcould not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.
On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.
Republican SenatorTom Cottonand GovernorSarah Huckabee Sanders- a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.
Trump names Stephen Miller as new  chief of staff
What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress
Exit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.
That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-PresidentJD Vanceand Secretary of StateMarco Rubio.
"The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.
Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.
Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.
Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.
In a lengthy post on X, SenatorTed Cruz, who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters.
"It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."
Florida GovernorRon DeSantis, who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.
White House denies Hegseth and Rubio to leave jobs after Republican election losses
Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
Both the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.
Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.
El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.
His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election.
"The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.
Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representativeAlexandria Ocasio-Cortezto run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."
Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.
This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.
Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.
Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.
Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide
Both parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.
Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds.
Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.
Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".
That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm.
"Neither party owns these voters," she said.
Texas has a new Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa
The Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.
Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend.
"Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said.
"After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

title: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
summary: One child and one young adult were killed in the crash, local authorities say, with more injured.
body:
French gendarmes and rescue workers at the scene of the crash in Lent, eastern France
A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.
The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent.
The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and at least 13 others have sustained minor injuries.
French President Emmanuel Macron said his thoughts were with the victims, the injured, and their families.
In a post on X, he said the nation stood by their side and thanked the rescue teams involved.
The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".
The two people killed have been identified by authorities. However, there have been differing reports as to the age of the girl.
The prosecutor's office said it was "opening an investigation into the incident, on charges of road homicide and aggravated road traffic injuries".
The driver has been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police. French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said initial tests indicated there were no traces of alcohol or drugs in his blood.
Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.
Local mayor Cristin told BFM TV: "I arrived minutes after the accident and people were in shock.
"The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured."
Addressing weather conditions at the time of the crash, the mayor told Le Figaro "there was a bit of fog, the road was wet" but there were "no major difficulties".
Speaking to the same paper, Fabrice Pannekoucke, head of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, said: "At this stage, there are no particular explanations or interpretations that can be given."
Tabarot said the bus did not operate "exclusively on school routes" but that there were "many schoolchildren on board".
Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot (centre) arrived at the scene following the crash
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the accident was tragic, and thanked the firefighters, medical teams and police who attended the scene.
Earlier, French Education Minister Édouard Geffray said it was "always difficult when our children are victims of accidents of this nature".
Emergency services were at the scene and medical helicopters were deployed to take victims with serious injuries to a specialised hospital.
More than 100 firefighters and 50 gendarmes were also at the scene.
The local town hall was opened to provide shelter and coordinate with emergency services, the local mayor said.

title: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines
summary: No link has been established between the threats against the airlines and those against the media outlets.
body:
European airlines have again been hit with a new wave of bomb threats - in the third such incident this week.
On Friday multiple flights to and from Lisbon, Rome, Prague and Sofia were targeted and the threats saw three planes escorted by Hungarian fighter jets, authorities said.
It also saw a number of high-profile media organisations,including Ireland's public broadcaster RTÉ, evacuated after threats were made against them - although there has been no concrete links between the messages against airlines and the broadcasters.
The disruption comes after nearly 30 aircraft and several airports across Europe were impacted by threatsearlier this week, in what the UK called a "malicious hoax".
Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats
A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, according to AFP.
France also reported at least four of its flights were targeted by threats, however they all landed safely.
No explosives have been found on any planes as of Friday.
As airlines were dealing with this latest wave of threats, several media outlets, including RTÉ, were evacuated after similar warnings were made against them.
Staff at the Irish Independent newspaper and the Dublin offices of radio stations NewstalkFM and TodayFM, were also advised to leave their buildings and UK broadcaster Sky said it also received a security threat.
In a statement, gardaí (Irish police) said they were "aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe".
Armed gardaí were deployed to RTÉ'S Dublin headquarter after a bomb threat
While no link has been established between the threats against airlines and media outlets, the Irish government has warned it is a "likely coordinated campaign of disruption".
In a statement, it said: "Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or co-ordinated effort.
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin described the situation as "worrying" and added his government's first priority was the safety of the Irish public.
"Yesterday, there appeared to be coordinated efforts to disrupt air travel," he said.
Martin told RTÉ it was not yet known if the threats had come from individuals or if it was a "coordinated attack" but said they were being taken seriously.
Ireland is scheduled to host two high-profile European Union meetings in Dublin next week.
Broadcaster Sky confirmed it had received a security threat, hours after RTÉ had evacuated its building.
The broadcaster, which is owned by Comcast, said in a statement read by a presenter on its news channel that the broadcaster had "carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities".
"The safety and security of our colleagues is our primary concern, and we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure."
Friday's disruption comes after the Russian extremist group "Male State", named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports,denied any link to the false warnings.
Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.
"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"

title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
summary: Paul Mackenzie ordered his followers to starve their children to death in a forest so they could "meet Jesus".
body:
Paul Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", the judge said last month
A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.
Alongside 28 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".
Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie bore the "primary criminal culpability" for ordering his followers to fast to death, in one of the world's deadliest episodes of cult activity.
"The sentence is appropriate and just, to send an unmistakable message that such atrocities warrant the maximum penalties allowed by law," the judge added.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.
The court sentenced Mackenzie to 100 years in prison for homicide and another 100 years for offences related to starvation.
The sentences within each category will run concurrently, but the two sets will run consecutively, bringing his total prison term to 200 years.
Mackenzie also faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he denies.
Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, arguing that the scale and circumstances of the killings warranted the harshest punishment.
However, Justice Mochache declined to impose the death penalty, despite ruling that the case met the threshold for its consideration.
"Nevertheless, the court declines the invitation to impose the death penalty on any of the victims," she said, adding that capital punishment would eliminate any prospect of rehabilitation and disengagement. The death sentence has not been carried out in Kenya since 1987.
Mackenzie was tried alongside 28 accomplices, including guards who enforced his fasting orders and gravediggers who helped conceal the victims' bodies in mass graves.
They received varying prison sentences of up to 160 years.
Justice Mochache described the killings as "cold and calculated", saying the perpetrators had shown no remorse and had even declared their willingness to fast to death themselves.
Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives including two grandchildren in Shakahola forest, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest".
Mackenzie and the co-accused had asked for leniency from the court.
Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.
More than 400 bodies were dug up in Shakahola forest
Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month.
Those who opposed Mackenzie's teachings were beaten to death.
One of his co-accused said he had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".
Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings" and those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus" the judge said.
The judge found that the deaths arose from an organised system, including religious teachings and directives that compelled followers to follow the deadly fasting.
Post-mortem results showed the cause of deaths to be starvation for most victims, while others died from suffocation, strangulation or head injuries.
The cause of death could not be determined for some, with their bodies having decomposed, while others died soon after their rescue as they were so emaciated.
The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.
Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) revealed that local administration and law enforcement officials had repeatedly turned a blind eye to the cult's activities.
"We expected at that time the police would take action immediately to go and rescue the other members there, but it didn't happen," said Wanje, who reported the case to the police in March 2023.
Wanje said a relative of his in the police force and a former cult participant had managed to save his grandson at the time. The child told the police what had happened and showed them the grave of his siblings.
"It was [supposed to be] his last day.. they [would have killed] my grandson."
The cult leader had previously been arrested and later released for lack of evidence.
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003.
Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers in its branches across Kenya.
The church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
The main church shut down in 2019 and Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.
While the conclusion of the murder cases may bring a sense of justice for the victims and their families, the convictions only account for 191 victims, while more than 400 bodies were exhumed from the forest.

title: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
summary: Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat election victory would mean slower AI development.
body:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday,ending the day up 1.1%,partlyreversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies,closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Averagewas flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.
Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
Pierre Baqué, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.
"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.
"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1%from 4.2% in September.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

title: Why the US midterms sparked an AI stock selloff
summary: Fears of more AI regulation appear to have sparked fear among investors, but  concerns about the industry have been growing for some time.
body:
Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check?
That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets.
The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple.
It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's midterm elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress.
A number of leading Democrats campaigned against the unhindered expansion of data centres, which have underpinned the growth of artificial intelligence.
Fears this will lead to more regulation of AI appear to have concerned investors. But worries about the industry's prospects have been growing for some time.
The release of Chat GPT by Open AI in late 2022 is widely seen as having generated massive public and corporate interest in the practical uses of AI. It also sparked a modern-day gold rush.
Investors flocked to put their money into companies producing computer chips and  networking infrastructure, building data centres and providing the energy to power them, as well as developing the AI itself. The value of tech companies soared.
The boom continued into this year. Investments in AI are expected to reach $1trillion in 2026 alone according to research by Goldman Sachs. The sector has scooped up so much available cash that other industries have seen their own borrowing costs increase as a result.
But investors want returns, and in recent months concerns have been growing about whether the AI boom can produce the expected riches.
Those worries have emerged at a time when public comments from AI researchers casting doubt over the safety of artificial intelligence - even suggesting it could represent an existential threat to humanity - have been grabbing headlines and fuelling speculation that a clampdown could lie ahead.
US tech stocks edge back up after AI slowdown fears sent value of firms plummeting
How does it affect me if share prices fall?
These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into grassroots concerns about the expansion of data centres and their impact on local communities.
These were largely focused on the facilities' high consumption of water and electricity, which many feared would push up their household bills – as well as the noise, use of land, and general disruption associated with them.
A Gallup poll published in May showed 71% of Americans would oppose the building of a data centre in their community. The figure for a nuclear power station was 53%.
James Talarico, who won the Senate race in once staunchly Republican Texas, was one of those to respond to this scepticism.
"While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn," he said.
"We must protect Americans and establish clear, consistent laws for businesses."
With control of both houses of Congress, Democrats are now expected to challenge the president's technology agenda more vigorously, while introducing legislation which could curb the expansion of the industry.
Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against data centres, pledging a moratorium on the construction of new facilities.
Hinojosa's win could present opposition to tech multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who has moved large parts of SpaceX and Tesla's operations to the state, for years a Republican stronghold.
The Tesla boss had spent nearly $450m to back Republican campaigns in the midterms.
As the co-founder of the British-based technology firm Arm Holdings, Tudor Brown, points out, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings". If the rewards are not likely to be as great as expected, some investors will choose to sell up.
The falls seen on stock markets over the past 24 hours would appear to have been triggered by the midterm results. But concerns that tech firms have become overvalued were being expressed long before the elections.
The question now is whether this is simply the removal of froth from an over-exuberant market, or a sign that the AI rush is a bubble about to burst, with much wider consequences.
Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights thinks investors will assess whether the political shift could result in restrictions on data centre construction, energy consumption and the deployment of AI technology.
She adds there is unlikely to be an immediate widespread recovery in tech stocks as traders are likely to be more selective, favouring firms with stronger balance sheets.
Brown thinks the impact will be limited. Share valuations, he thinks, were inflated by expectations of "almost infinite AI growth", which have been followed by "a bit of a panic".
"There is a natural floor to this", he says. "After that it will reflect I think that actually there's still a lot of money being made in these companies".

title: How does it affect me if share prices fall?
summary: Changes in the FTSE 100 and other indexes are not just for financial experts, they can affect our lives.
body:
Major tech firms have seen their stock values fall after a sell-off by investors following the US midterm elections.
The fall in the value of their shares across the world has been blamed on an expectation of a slowdown in AI development, although it comes after sharp rises over recent years.
As companies grow, they may issue shares. Many of the largest companies in the UK have shares which are bought and sold on the London Stock Exchange.
Their collective performance is often quoted amid a blizzard of numbers that may feel confusing and irrelevant.
Booms or falls in the stock market make the news, but rarely does anyone mention the FTSE 100 during a coffee with friends.
Yet, there are good reasons why this performance affects your life and finances.
Many people's initial reaction to "the markets" is that they are not directly affected, because they do not invest money.
Yet there are millions of people with a pension - either private or through work - who will see their savings (in what is known as a defined contribution pension) invested by pension schemes. The value of their savings pot is influenced by the performance of these investments.
Pension savers mostly let experts choose where to invest this money to help it grow. Widespread falls in share prices are likely to be bad news for pension savers.
Hundreds of billions of pounds are held in defined contribution pensions at the moment.
So big rises or falls can affect your pension, but the advice is to remember that pension savings, like any investments, are usually a long-term bet.
Experts say that investors have always had to ride economic shocks. Investments, by definition, require a long-term outlook and strategy. So, they are urging people not to panic in such circumstances or make knee-jerk decisions.
Some people have a pension which promises a specific value, depending on their salary. Others have no pension at all.
Millions of people have been automatically enrolled into a pension and may have not really noticed. Those schemes see employers divert wages into a pension and contribute some money themselves. The government adds a little in tax relief.
In every case, the value of these pension savings is affected by investment performance. So "the markets" matter - maybe not as much as everyday wages, but for future pensions.
Timing is more critical for those at retirement age, as this may be when a retiree uses their pension pot to buy a retirement income, or annuity. The bigger the pot, the more income they will get in retirement.
As you approach retirement age, pension pots tend to be moved to less risky investments, such as government bonds. When stock markets fall, these bonds can do better.
Anyone who has a pension pot invested and is taking an income from it will again see their investment go up and down with the stock markets.
That could mean getting less than you expected if you cash in too much after stock markets have fallen, making it important to plan how to make up any of this shortfall, experts say.
However, higher interest rates tend to mean better rates offered on annuities, and there is a chance of more rate rises in the UK by the Bank of England.
If share prices fall for an extended period then that could have an effect on jobs.
That's because investors in the company expect a return on that investment.
When it falls for a while, then they would expect the business to address issues, for example by cutting costs, and therefore jobs.
There is a huge element of the unknown here though. Companies have to consider lots of factors when making decisions on investment and employment.
In purely investment terms, lower share prices can offer an opportunity to buy, in the hope that over the long term, they recover and rise. Many people will do this initially through a stocks and shares Individual Savings Account (Isa).
However, it is worth noting that the sell-off in tech stocks in particular came after big rises, so long-term investors are still likely to have seen gains.
Experts and regulators are at pains to point out that investments can go down as well as up, and urge people not to put everything into one investment, but to diversify.
Some people invest money in what are known as tracker funds. These go up and down in line with the performance of a certain index, such as the FTSE 100.
So if the index falls, so does the value of their investments and vice versa. One advantage of these funds is that they often cost relatively little to sign up to.
Yes, and millions of people do, but experts stress that a long-term strategy is required to ride out short-term falls. It is also important to ensure cash savings are held too, so unexpected expenses - like the need for a replacement boiler - can be covered.
The government is keen to get people in the UK to invest more, partly because it says that will help UK economic growth and partly because it is much more popular among individuals in the US and some parts of Europe.
It backed an advertising campaign to encourage people to invest, funded by some of the UK's biggest financial services firms.
But the choice of "Savvy the Squirrel" to front the campaign has raised some eyebrows. Some question whether the push could get anywhere close to the success of the Tell Sid adverts of the 1980s, which encouraged people to invest in the newly privatised British Gas.
When we see big shifts in the stock markets there can also be fluctuations in the value of currencies and exchange rates.
As a result, prices could go up, but could also go down.
Upheaval to economies across the world, to oil prices and so on, have a big impact on what we pay at home for goods and services, so there are lots of factors in play.

title: Why smoky bacon crisps threaten to reignite rows over EU rules
summary: A post-Brexit deal on food standards has raised questions over the future naming of the classic British snack.
body:
The naming of smoky bacon-flavoured crisps has become the latest political headache to emerge from the government's bid for closer ties with the EU.
The government is negotiating a deal on food standards in a bid to cut costs for British companies trading with Europe.

title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
summary: Musk said it was to make room for production of its Cybercabs - autonomous taxis without a driver.
body:
Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.
He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.
But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."
With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.
Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it "the best vehicle Tesla has ever made,external" as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".
Musk responded to the user,externalwith the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."
Tesla's stock rose 4.7% on Friday after his announcement.
The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was "way more awesome than people realise,external" in March, and called it the "best product Tesla has ever made to date,external" in April.
But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.
It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.
Watch: The Cybertruck window stunt
Despite the gaffe, the Cybertruck ended up receiving a 146,000 orders,Musk said in 2019, while it was still in development.
In the end, the vehicle launched in 2023, keeping its novel design - an angular shape with a body made of stainless steel.
In 2025, Tesla sold just 20,237 Cybertrucks, a decline from 38,965 a year earlier, according to figures from Kelley Blue Book.
Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 after commercial production of Cybertruck began in 2023.
Tesla fans praised its retro-futuristic look, which some said looked like something "straight out of Blade Runner,external".
But critics were far less kind, joking about its appearance and labelling it "ugly as sin,external".
Several recalls -including in 2025affecting more than 46,000 Cybertrucks over concerns part of its trim could fall off - would not have helped.
And then there's the price.
"We need to make it at a price that people can afford,"Musk told Wall Street analysts that year- which ended up being $61,000 (then £48,000) for all the "bells and whistles".
In 2026, the so-called "Cyberbeast" model comes in at $102,000.

title: PM tells firms to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law
summary: The government argues the change will help jobseekers and could help to prevent pay discrimination.
body:
Andy Burnham says it isn't fair if an employer 'holds all the cards'
Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so.
The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible".
It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable.
It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog saidemployees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning.
Burnham said the current system felt "weighted against the applicant" and the changes were aimed at "tilting the scales back".
"It can be quite soul destroying for young people these days, applying for jobs when the salary is not listed but sometimes they're not getting a reply," he told the BBC.
The prime minister added that publishing salaries in adverts was also important for closing the gender pay gap.
He was also challenged over whether MPs should be disclosing salaries when advertising for staff in their offices.
A number of politiciansare currently advertising for roles without giving an expected salary.,external
Burnham said: "It would apply completely to them too and the call I'm making today is, before the law changes do it voluntarily because it's the right thing to do."
The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.
"Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Burnham said.
The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.
Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".
The proposals are similar tomeasures being introduced in the European Union.,external
Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.
According to data from UK jobs website Adzuna,external, 51% of the adverts on its site in September had salary information, but the proportion has been falling in recent years.
Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said being open about pay "should be the norm, not the exception".
He added that employers who put a salary on a job advert "attract more applicants, and better-suited ones".
Previous research from the CIPD,external, an industry body for human resources managers, has indicated that the public sector and charities are more likely to reveal pay information that private firms, while pay ranges were more common than specific salaries.
But it found not all employers were "fully transparent", with pay ranges sometimes wider than £10,000.
CIPD chief executive Neil Carberry said that while, in principle, giving salary details was "a good thing", in practice it was "more complicated".
"There isn't always a single fixed figure, and employers will want to set pay based on a candidate's skills, experience and potential."
Carberry added the process was complex, saying that drafting job adverts is "best left to good employer practice rather than government regulation".
The government has said it will set out further details on what information will be required and how the legislation will be enforced "in due course".
Conservative shadow business secretary Julia Lopez said: "At a time when employers are finding it harder and harder to take on staff, Labour have decided to make their lives even more difficult.
"It should be up to businesses to decide what information they advertise about job openings, and to decide how to attract the best applicants.
"As long as they are not being dishonest, misleading or discriminatory, it should not be a matter for the government."
Last week, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), said publishing salaries in job adverts would be a "positive step".
It also said bosses should be required to respond to questionnaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination.
At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about their co-workers.
The EHRC also said employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from continuing.
Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, butapplicants are under no obligation to tell them.

title: Burnham responds to BBC question over Labour's past links to Brand
summary: The prime minister says that Labour politicians courting the comedian a decade ago had not been aware of his crimes.
body:
In 2014 Burnham posted a supportive message on social media when Brand was facing media criticism about his housing arrangements
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russell Brand has rightly been held to account for his "horrific" crimes and sought to explain Labour's previous association with the comedian.
Some within the Labour Party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him - and in 2014 Burnham posted a supportive message on social media when the comedian was facing media criticism about his housing arrangements.
Asked about the 2014 tweet on Friday, Burnham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."
Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Thursday.
In 2014, Brand was writing regular opinion pieces for newspapers and appearing on political discussion programmes, including the BBC's Question Time.
His anti-establishment and left-wing views had also gained him a following on social media.
The same year, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted on Twitter in support of Brand following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.
It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his 2014 tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.
Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned for.
At the time, Burnham said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".
Asked about that social media post on Friday, Burnham told the BBC "all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do".
The PM added: "His [Brand's] crimes are horrific, he's rightly been held to account, justice for the victims and that is the right course that's been taken here.
"It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life, but what is important is that where there is wrongdoing it is exposed."
The prime minister added: "Credit to the victims, huge credit, the courage that it's taken, but also the journalists who've exposed this."
Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.
Brand, who had previously dismissed the idea of voting, backed Labour following the interview, saying Miliband had convinced him that "this bloke will listen to us".
Miliband, who is now foreign secretary, has previouslysaid he regrets being interviewed by Brand.
On Friday, a spokesman for Miliband told the BBC: "These are horrific crimes that Russell Brand has been found guilty of and Ed's profound sympathy is with the victims.
"As he said in 2023, 'of course, knowing what I know now - and I was not aware of these allegations at the time about Russell Brand - I wouldn't have done that interview and I regret doing it'."
Brand was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault.
During a four-week trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.
The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody before he is due to return to court on Monday for sentencing.

title: Policing needs reform to cope with modern criminals, Met Police chief warns
summary: The Met Police chief used a speech to argue that the current policing system in England and Wales is "heading for failure" without urgent change.
body:
Watch: 'Degradation of policing' by not reforming force, says Met chief
The police system in England and Wales cannot cope against sophisticated modern criminals without urgent reform, the head of the Metropolitan Police has said.
In a speech on Friday, Sir Mark Rowley argued the system was "heading for failure" without change.
He is proposing eight to 10 regional police forces, supported by hundreds of local policing commands and a new national force, in what would be the biggest overhaul of policing since the 1960s.
The changes would replace the 43-force structure with three tiers: local teams dealing with neighbourhood issues, regional forces sharing specialist resources and a National Police Service tackling the most serious crimes.
In January it seemed that the many senior police officers were in favour of creating a National Police Service, and that organising into much larger regional forces had won the argument.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmoodproduced a white paperthat aligned with their ideas and asked the former Metropolitan Police Commissioner Lord Hogan-Howe to look at what the force boundaries might be.
But everything changed in July when Andy Burnham became prime minister. So far, Burnham has not spoken publicly about the plans, and the police chiefs are nervous that they may not have his backing. That may be why they have come out so strongly today, warning of the potentially apocalyptic effect of doing nothing.
As well as pushing hard for large regional forces, they are also making an argument about money which is familiarfrom the defence funding argument.
Sir Mark also pointed out that police funding in England and Wales has fallen from 0.9% of GDP to 0.7%. Implicit in that is that while the slice of the cake being allocated to defending the country is growing, the slice being allocated to defending people's communities and their homes is getting smaller.
Labour wants to shake up the police - but will that solve 'everyday crime epidemic'?
Number of police forces to be cut in major shake-up
Court system under massive strain, warns Met chief
In his speech, Sir Mark saidorganised crime groups, fraud networks, cyber-criminals and those involved in online child abuse increasingly operate across regional and international borders, while police forces remain organised around local areas.
"The victim remains local but increasingly the threat does not," he said citing the example of children who are "groomed by predators on another continent".
He argued that the current system is struggling to keep pace with these threats, saying: "We have 43 overstretched forces trying to do too much, with too little."
Merging forces would reduce duplication and could free up thousands of roles to be redirected towards front line policing, he believes.
Speaking on BBC Breakfast prior to his speech, Sir Mark said crime had changed a lot over the years but the police was largely organised how it was 60 years ago.
"Obviously the world's moved on a long way in that time."
His proposals follow a consultation launched by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood in January. This included plans for a National Police Service to tackle the most complex crimes and a possible merger of the 43 forces into fewer, larger forces.
However some rural police and crime commissioners have described the plans as "political manoeuvring" by larger forces to "load the dice in their favour".
Dorset Police and Crime Commissioner David Sidwick reiterated his strong opposition to proposals to merge the forces.
"My concern is simple. If funding is diverted away from frontline services in Dorset to establish new national structures, local communities could end up receiving less rather than more."
In addition, Kent's Conservative police and crime commissioner Matthew Scott said: "[Sir Mark believes] policing should suffer a decade of disruption, that local policing services should be cut back and made more remote, and that this can all be done without ever asking the public what they want from their local police force."
The Association of Police and Crime Commissioners (APCC) has also questioned whether merging forces is the best way to improve policing.
It said: "The case for modernisation and a National Police Service is clear. The case for reducing 43 forces to nine regional 'mega-forces' is not."
Outgoing Cheshire Chief Constable Mark Roberts also said a future policing model needs to be built in a way that retains the places that already work well so that they do not "get subsumed" and end up "scrabbling to try and get resource from some of the metropolitan areas"
"Bigger isn't always better - we see some high performing big forces, we see some poorer performing big forces.
"The aim is to raise everyone at least to the minimum standard of the best," Roberts said after Rowley's speech.
Asked on Breakfast what would happen if the reforms were not put in place, Sir Mark said: "the risk is failure".
"Failure means solving fewer crimes, less local presence, when you get exceptional incidents like a certain outbreak of disorder like we saw in Hampshire."
In September police clashed withanti-migrant protesters in Portsmouthwhen 120 migrants arrived in a single dinghy.
"Standing still looks like a degradation of policing day by day, struggling even more as criminals outpace policing because we're not organised to meet it," Sir Mark added.
A Home Office spokesperson defended the plans, saying: "Our current model of policing has not changed since the 1960s and is no longer fit for purpose."
Sir Mark has also highlighted the financial pressures facing policing, saying that spending on policing had fallen from about 0.9% of GDP to 0.7% since 2010, which he said was as "a big hit".
"We do need investment as well, but if you threw loads of money at the current system it's still not going to fix the fundamental problem, it's not designed to meet today's challenges," he told the BBC.
"Throwing money at the current system isn't going to work."
Sir Mark said in his speech that years of underinvestment hasleft forces relying on ageing technology, and officers are increasingly diverted from neighbourhood policing to deal with other demands, including mental health and social care.
He also pointedto falling police performance, saying positive outcomes nationally are now less than half the level they were 12 years ago, while public confidence has fallen by 9%.
